title: Tashlich, casting away
hookLine: Jews cast crumbs into flowing water, symbolizing sins cast away (Micah 7:19)

cards: An afternoon by a river. People in the kind of clothes you'd wear to synagogue stand along the bank, some holding small prayer books. A grandfather lifts a child so she can see over the rail.

Someone tosses a few crumbs of bread onto the water, and the current carries them downstream. A woman turns her coat pockets inside out and shakes them over the edge. Nobody is feeding the ducks, exactly.
They're acting out a line from one of the prophets, about where wrongs go.

teach.b: First, the verse. The prophet Micah ends his book with a question and a promise.

In the King James words: "Who is a God like unto thee, that pardoneth iniquity, and passeth by the transgression of the remnant of his heritage? he retaineth not his anger for ever, because he delighteth in mercy."
And then: "He will turn again, he will have compassion upon us; he will subdue our iniquities; and thou wilt cast all their sins into the depths of the sea." Second, the name.
In Micah's Hebrew, the word for thou wilt cast gives the custom its name: tashlich.
On Rosh Hashanah, in the afternoon, Jews in some places walk to flowing water, a river, a stream, the sea, and say verses from Micah and the Psalms. Some toss crumbs; some shake out their pockets.
Third, what the crumbs are. The bread doesn't carry the sins away by itself. In the tradition's own telling, the turning back, the teshuvah, is the work.
The crumbs are a picture of it, something for the hands to do: you watch the thing go where you can't reach it anymore.

teach.h: INTO THE DEPTHS OF THE SEA.
teach.b: Fourth, the end of a stretch. Tashlich closes the Jewish voices on forgiveness: the return, four steps, ask them first, Joseph weeping, Esau running, ten days, and now the river.
Notice who does the casting in Micah's verse. Not the person. God casts the sins into the depths, and the depths, in the verse's picture, are a place nobody goes to fish them back out.

how: On the afternoon of Rosh Hashanah, some Jews go to a river, stream or sea to recite verses from Micah and the Psalms; some toss bread crumbs onto the water, and some shake out their pockets.

o: feeding the birds by a river as an act of charity
casting crumbs on flowing water, a picture of wrongs cast away
the blessing said over bread at the new year's meal

s: Micah says God keeps his anger forever
"he retaineth not his anger for ever, because he delighteth in mercy."
tashlich is done at flowing water
a river, a stream or the sea, on the afternoon of Rosh Hashanah.
in Micah's verse, the person casts their own sins into the sea
"thou wilt cast all their sins into the depths of the sea": God does the casting.

games.q: it's Rosh Hashanah afternoon, and you're at the river's edge with nothing in your pockets. what do people at tashlich do?
o: go home; without bread it doesn't count.
say the verses, and shake out your pockets.
throw something heavy into the water.
games.why: some toss crumbs and some just shake out their pockets. the crumbs are a picture; the turning back is the work.

practice: If there's water near you, even a bowl on the table, bring a leaf or a small scrap close; if not, picture one.

Give it one thing you're ready to put down, a resentment, a regret, an old wrong you've already turned from, then let it drop onto the water, or let it go in your mind, and watch it drift without reaching for it.
If you pray, you can say a line from Micah.

wordCard.voice: Tashlich. Hebrew, from Micah's thou wilt cast: the custom on Rosh Hashanah of going to flowing water and casting crumbs, a picture of wrongs cast away. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: thou wilt cast, from Micah 7:19; the name of the custom.

carryVoice: Your line: cast it away. Into the depths, where nobody fishes. That's day nine hundred forty-six.
